• Japanese Pharmacopoeia
Vomiting
Vomiting (scientifically known as emesis, and otherwise known as puking, and throwing up) is the forceful expulsion of
the contents of one's <color=#3366CC>stomach</color> through the <color=#3366CC>mouth</color> and sometimes the <color=#3366CC>nose</color>. The vomited contents are known as vomit
or vomitus.

Vomiting can be the result of ailments such as <color=#3366CC>food poisoning</color>, <color=#3366CC>gastroenteritis</color>, <color=#3366CC>pregnancy</color>, <color=#3366CC>motion sickness</color>, or
hangover; or it can be an after effect of diseases such as <color=#3366CC>brain tumors</color>, elevated intracranial pressure, or overexposure
to <color=#3366CC>ionizing radiation</color>. The feeling that one is about to vomit is called <color=#3366CC>nausea</color>; it often precedes, but does not always lead
to vomiting. Impairment due to <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color>, <color=#3366CC>anesthesia</color>, or other <color=#3366CC>sedatives</color> can cause inhalation of vomit. In severe cases,
where <color=#3366CC>dehydration</color> develops, <color=#3366CC>intravenous</color> fluid may be required. Antiemetics are sometimes necessary to suppress
nausea and vomiting. Self-induced vomiting can be a component of an eating disorder such as <color=#3366CC>bulimia nervosa</color>, and is
itself now classified as an eating disorder on its own, purging disorder.
Complications
Aspiration
Vomiting is dangerous if gastric content enters the respiratory tract. Under normal circumstances, the gag reflex and
<color=#3366CC>coughing</color> prevent this from occurring; however, these protective reflexes are compromised in persons who are under
the influence of certain substances (including <color=#3366CC>alcohol</color>) or even mildly <color=#3366CC>anesthetized</color>. The individual may choke and
<color=#3366CC>asphyxiate</color> or develop aspiration pneumonia.
Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
Prolonged and excessive vomiting depletes the body of <color=#3366CC>water</color> (<color=#3366CC>dehydration</color>), and may alter the <color=#3366CC>electrolyte</color> status.
Gastric vomiting leads to the loss of acid and chloride directly. Combined with the resulting alkaline tide, this leads to
hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis (low <color=#3366CC>chloride</color> levels together with high HCO3- and CO2 and increased blood <color=#3366CC>pH</color>) and
often hypokalemia (<color=#3366CC>potassium</color> depletion). The hypokalemia is an indirect result of the <color=#3366CC>kidney</color> compensating for the loss
of acid. With the loss of intake of food the individual may eventually become cachectic. A less frequent occurrence
results from a vomiting of intestinal contents, including bile acids and HCO3-.
Mallory–Weiss tear
Repeated or profuse vomiting may cause erosions to the <color=#3366CC>esophagus</color> or small tears in the esophageal mucosa
(Mallory–Weiss tear). This may become apparent if fresh red blood is mixed with vomit after several episodes.
Dentistry
Recurrent vomiting, such as observed in <color=#3366CC>bulimia nervosa</color> or more rarely <color=#3366CC>anorexia nervosa</color>, may lead to the destruction
of the tooth enamel due to the acidity of the vomit. Digestive enzymes can also have a negative effect on oral health, by
degrading the tissue of the <color=#3366CC>gums</color>.
Pathophysiology
Receptors on the floor of the fourth ventricle of the brain represent a chemoreceptor trigger zone, known as the area
postrema, stimulation of which can lead to vomiting. The area postrema is a circumventricular organ and as such lies
outside the <color=#3366CC>blood–brain barrier</color>; it can therefore be stimulated by blood-borne drugs that can <color=#3366CC>stimulate vomiting</color> or
inhibit it.
There are various sources of input to the vomiting center:
• The chemoreceptor trigger zone at the base of the fourth ventricle has numerous dopamine D2 receptors,
serotonin 5-HT3 receptors, opioid receptors, acetylcholine receptors, and receptors for substance P. Stimulation of
different receptors are involved in different pathways leading to emesis, in the final common pathway substance P
appears involved.
• The <color=#3366CC>vestibular system</color>, which sends information to the brain via cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve), plays a
major role in <color=#3366CC>motion sickness</color>, and is rich in muscarinic receptors and histamine H1 receptors.
• The <color=#3366CC>cranial nerve X</color> (<color=#3366CC>vagus nerve</color>) is activated when the <color=#3366CC>pharynx</color> is irritated, leading to a gag reflex.
• The vagal and enteric nervous system inputs transmit information regarding the state of the <color=#3366CC>gastrointestinal</color>

<color=#3366CC>system</color>. Irritation of the GI mucosa by <color=#3366CC>chemotherapy</color>, <color=#3366CC>radiation</color>, distention, or acute infectious <color=#3366CC>gastroenteritis</color>
activates the 5-HT3 receptors of these inputs.
• The <color=#3366CC>CNS</color> mediates vomiting that arises from psychiatric disorders and stress from higher brain centers.
• The <color=#3366CC>medulla</color> plays an important role for triggering the vomiting act.
The vomiting act encompasses three types of outputs initiated by the chemoreceptor trigger zone: Motor,
<color=#3366CC>parasympathetic nervous system</color> (PNS), and <color=#3366CC>sympathetic nervous system</color> (SNS). They are as follows:
• Increased <color=#3366CC>salivation</color> to protect tooth enamel from stomach acids. (Excessive vomiting leads to dental erosion.) This
is part of the PNS output.
• The body takes a deep breath to avoid aspirating vomit.
• Retroperistalsis starts from the middle of the <color=#3366CC>small intestine</color> and sweeps up digestive tract contents into the
stomach, through the relaxed pyloric sphincter.
• Intrathoracic pressure lowers (by inspiration against a closed glottis), coupled with an increase in abdominal
pressure as the <color=#3366CC>abdominal muscles</color> contract, propels stomach contents into the <color=#3366CC>esophagus</color> as the <color=#3366CC>lower</color>
<color=#3366CC>esophageal sphincter</color> relaxes. The stomach itself does not contract in the process of vomiting except for at the
angular notch, nor is there any retroperistalsis in the esophagus.
• Vomiting is ordinarily preceded by retching.
• Vomiting also initiates an <color=#3366CC>SNS</color> response causing both sweating and increased heart rate.
Phases
The vomiting act has two phases. In the retching phase, the abdominal muscles undergo a few rounds of coordinated
contractions together with the diaphragm and the muscles used in respiratory inspiration. For this reason, an individual
may confuse this phase with an episode of violent <color=#3366CC>hiccups</color>. In this retching phase, nothing has yet been expelled. In the
next phase, also termed the expulsive phase, intense pressure is formed in the stomach brought about by enormous
shifts in both the diaphragm and the abdomen. These shifts are, in essence, vigorous contractions of these muscles
that last for extended periods of time—much longer than a normal period of muscular contraction. The pressure is then
suddenly released when the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes resulting in the expulsion of gastric contents. As the
mouth and nasal cavity are connected via the back of the throat, particularly forceful vomiting, or producing large
quantities of vomit may result in material being ejected through the <color=#3366CC>nostrils</color> in addition to the mouth. Individuals who do
not regularly exercise their abdominal muscles may experience pain in those muscles for a few days. The decrease in
pressure and the release of endorphins into the bloodstream after the expulsion causes the vomiter to feel relief almost
immediately after vomiting.
Contents
Gastric secretions and likewise vomit are highly <color=#3366CC>acidic</color>. Recent food intake appears in the gastric vomit. Irrespective of
the content, vomit tends to be <color=#3366CC>malodorous</color>.
The content of the vomitus (vomit) may be of medical interest. Fresh <color=#3366CC>blood</color> in the vomit is termed hematemesis ("blood
vomiting"). Altered blood bears resemblance to coffee grounds (as the <color=#3366CC>iron</color> in the blood is <color=#3366CC>oxidized</color>) and, when this
matter is identified, the term coffee-ground vomiting is used. <color=#3366CC>Bile</color> can enter the vomit during subsequent heaves due to
<color=#3366CC>duodenal</color> contraction if the vomiting is severe. Fecal vomiting is often a consequence of intestinal obstruction or a
gastrocolic <color=#3366CC>fistula</color> and is treated as a warning sign of this potentially serious problem (signum mali ominis).
If the vomiting reflex continues for an extended period with no appreciable vomitus, the condition is known as
non-productive emesis or "dry heaves", which can be painful and debilitating.
Color of vomit
• Bright red in the vomit suggests bleeding from the esophagus
• Dark red vomit with liver-like clots suggests profuse bleeding in the stomach, such as from a perforated ulcer
• Coffee-ground-like vomit suggests less severe bleeding in the stomach because the gastric acid has had time to
change the composition of the blood
• Yellow or green vomit suggests bile, indicating that the pyloric valve is open and bile is flowing into the stomach
from the duodenum. This may occur during successive episodes of vomiting after the stomach contents have been
completely expelled.
Causes
Vomiting may be due to a large number of causes, and vomiting has a long differential diagnosis.
Digestive tract
Causes in the <color=#3366CC>digestive tract</color>
• Gastritis (<color=#3366CC>inflammation</color> of the gastric wall)
• <color=#3366CC>Gastroenteritis</color>
• Gastroesophageal reflux disease
• Celiac disease
• Non-celiac gluten sensitivity
• Pyloric stenosis (in babies, this typically causes a very forceful "projectile vomiting" and is an indication for urgent
surgery)
• Bowel obstruction
• Overeating (stomach too full)
• Acute abdomen and/or peritonitis
• Ileus
• <color=#3366CC>Food allergies</color> (often in conjunction with <color=#3366CC>hives</color> or swelling)
• Cholecystitis, pancreatitis, <color=#3366CC>appendicitis</color>, <color=#3366CC>hepatitis</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Food poisoning</color>
• In children, it can be caused by an <color=#3366CC>allergic reaction</color> to cow's <color=#3366CC>milk proteins</color> (milk allergy or <color=#3366CC>lactose intolerance</color>)
Sensory system and brain
Causes in the <color=#3366CC>sensory system</color>:
• Movement leading to <color=#3366CC>motion sickness</color> (which is caused by overstimulation of the labyrinthine canals of the ear)
• Ménière's disease
• <color=#3366CC>Vertigo</color>
Causes in the <color=#3366CC>brain</color>:
• <color=#3366CC>Concussion</color>
• Cerebral hemorrhage
• Cerebral aneurysm
• <color=#3366CC>Migraine</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Brain tumors</color>, which can cause the chemoreceptors to malfunction
• Benign intracranial hypertension and hydrocephalus
<color=#3366CC>Metabolic</color> disturbances (these may irritate both the stomach and the parts of the brain that coordinate vomiting):
• Hypercalcemia (high calcium levels)
• Uremia (<color=#3366CC>urea</color> accumulation, usually due to <color=#3366CC>kidney failure</color>)
• Adrenal insufficiency
• Hypoglycemia
• Hyperglycemia
• <color=#3366CC>Endometriosis</color>
<color=#3366CC>Pregnancy</color>:
• Hyperemesis, morning sickness
Drug reaction (vomiting may occur as an acute somatic response to):
• <color=#3366CC>Alcohol</color>, which can be partially oxidized into <color=#3366CC>acetaldehyde</color> that causes the symptoms of hangover, including
nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, and fast heart rate.
• <color=#3366CC>Opioids</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors</color>
• Many <color=#3366CC>chemotherapy</color> drugs
• Some entheogens (such as peyote or ayahuasca)
High altitude:
• Altitude sickness
<color=#3366CC>Illness</color> (sometimes colloquially known as "<color=#3366CC>stomach flu</color>"—a broad name that refers to gastric inflammation caused by a
range of viruses and bacteria):
• <color=#3366CC>Norovirus</color> (formerly Norwalk virus or Norwalk agent)
• Swine influenza (H1N1)
Psychiatric/behavioral:
• <color=#3366CC>Bulimia nervosa</color>
• Food neophobia
• Purging disorder
Emetics
An emetic, such as syrup of ipecac, is a substance that induces vomiting when administered orally or by injection. An
emetic is used medically when a substance has been ingested and must be expelled from the body immediately. For
this reason, many toxic and easily digestible products such as rat poison contain an emetic. This presents no problem
for the effectiveness of the <color=#3366CC>rodenticide</color> as rodents are unable to vomit. Inducing vomiting can remove the substance
before it is absorbed into the body. Emetics can be divided into two categories: those that produce their effect by acting
on the vomiting center in the medulla, and those that act directly on the stomach itself. Some emetics, such as ipecac,
fall into both categories: they initially act directly on the stomach, while their further and more vigorous effect occurs by
stimulation of the medullary center.
<color=#3366CC>Salt</color> water and mustard water, which act directly on the stomach, have been used since ancient times as emetics. Care
must be taken with salt, as excessive intake can potentially be harmful. <color=#3366CC>Copper sulfate</color> was also used in the past as an
emetic. It is now considered too toxic for this use.
<color=#3366CC>Hydrogen peroxide</color> is used as an emetic in veterinary practice.
Self-induced
• <color=#3366CC>Eating disorders</color> (<color=#3366CC>anorexia nervosa</color> or <color=#3366CC>bulimia nervosa</color>)
• To eliminate an ingested poison (some poisons should not be vomited as they may be more toxic when inhaled or
aspirated; it is better to ask for help before inducing vomiting)
• Participants in milk chugging typically end up vomiting most of the milk they consume, as proteins in the ingested
milk (such as casein) rapidly denature and unravel on contact with gastric acid and protease enzymes, rapidly
filling the stomach. Once the stomach becomes full, stretch receptors in the stomach wall trigger signals to vomit to
expel any further liquid the participant ingests.
• People suffering from <color=#3366CC>nausea</color> may induce vomiting in hopes of feeling better.
Miscellaneous
• After <color=#3366CC>surgery</color> (postoperative nausea and vomiting)
• Disagreeable sights or <color=#3366CC>disgust</color>, smells, tastes, sounds or thoughts (such as decayed matter, others' vomit, thinking
of vomiting), etc.
• Extreme pain, such as an intense <color=#3366CC>headache</color> or <color=#3366CC>myocardial infarction</color> (heart attack)
• Extreme <color=#3366CC>emotions</color>
• Cyclic vomiting syndrome (a poorly understood condition with attacks of vomiting)
• Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (similar to cyclic vomiting syndrome, but has cannabis use as its underlying
cause).
• High doses of <color=#3366CC>ionizing radiation</color> sometimes trigger a vomit reflex.
• Violent fits of <color=#3366CC>coughing</color>, <color=#3366CC>hiccups</color>, or <color=#3366CC>asthma</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Anxiety</color>
• <color=#3366CC>Depression</color>
• Overexertion (doing too much strenuous exercise can lead to vomiting shortly afterwards).
Other types
• Projectile vomiting is vomiting that ejects the gastric contents with great force. It is a classic symptom of infantile
hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, in which it typically follows feeding and can be so forceful that some material exits
through the nose.
Treatment
An antiemetic is a <color=#3366CC>drug</color> that is effective against vomiting and <color=#3366CC>nausea</color>. Antiemetics are typically used to treat <color=#3366CC>motion</color>
<color=#3366CC>sickness</color> and the <color=#3366CC>side effects</color> of medications such as <color=#3366CC>opioids</color> and <color=#3366CC>chemotherapy</color>.
Antiemetics act by inhibiting the receptor sites associated with emesis. Hence, anticholinergics, antihistamines,
dopamine antagonists, serotonin antagonists, and cannabinoids are used as antiemetics.
Evidence to support the use of antiemetics for nausea and vomiting among adults in the <color=#3366CC>emergency department</color> is
poor. It is unclear if any medication is better than another or better than no active treatment.
Epidemiology
<color=#3366CC>Nausea</color> and/or vomiting are the main complaints in 1.6% of visits to family physicians in Australia.
Society and culture
<color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color>, writing on the culture of the <color=#3366CC>ancient Persians</color> and highlighting the differences with those of the <color=#3366CC>Greeks</color>,
notes that to vomit in the presence of others is prohibited among Persians.
Social cues
It is quite common that, when one person vomits, others nearby become nauseated, particularly when smelling the
vomit of others, and often to the point of vomiting themselves. This tendency in human populations has been observed
at drinking parties, where excessive consumption of <color=#3366CC>alcoholic beverages</color> may cause a number of party members to
vomit nearly simultaneously, triggered by the initial vomiting of a single member of the party.
Intense vomiting in ayahuasca ceremonies is a common phenomenon. However, people who experience "la purga"
after drinking ayahuasca, in general, regard the practise as both a physical and spiritual cleanse and often come to
welcome it. It has been suggested that the consistent emetic effects of ayahuasca—in addition to its many other
therapeutic properties—was of medicinal benefit to <color=#3366CC>indigenous peoples</color> of the Amazon, in helping to clear <color=#3366CC>parasites</color>
from the gastrointestinal system.
There have also been documented cases of a single ill and vomiting individual inadvertently causing others to vomit,
when they are especially fearful of also becoming ill, through a form of <color=#3366CC>mass hysteria</color>.
Most people try to contain their vomit by vomiting into a sink, toilet, or trash can, as vomit is difficult and unpleasant to
clean. On airplanes and boats, special bags are supplied for sick passengers to vomit into. A special disposable bag
(leakproof, puncture-resistant, odorless) containing absorbent material that solidifies the vomit quickly is also available,
making it convenient and safe to store until there is an opportunity to dispose of it conveniently.
People who vomit chronically (e.g., as part of an <color=#3366CC>eating disorder</color> such as <color=#3366CC>bulimia nervosa</color>) may devise various ways to
hide this disorder.
An online study of people's responses to "horrible sounds" found vomiting "the most disgusting". Professor Trevor Cox
of the University of Salford's Acoustic Research Centre said, "We are pre-programmed to be repulsed by horrible things
such as vomiting, as it is fundamental to staying alive to avoid nasty stuff." It is thought that <color=#3366CC>disgust</color> is triggered by the
sound of vomiting to protect those nearby from possibly diseased food.
Psychology
Emetophilia is sexual arousal from vomiting, or watching others vomit. Emetophobia is a phobia that causes
overwhelming, intense anxiety pertaining to vomiting.
